title: How does memory work?
subtitle: The brain
subject: sciences
description: Memory is not a camera. Every recollection is rebuilt. Here is how the brain encodes, stores, and sometimes invents.

hero.hook: Remembering is not reopening a file. It is rebuilding a scene.

blocks.text: We often picture memory as a hard drive: you record, you file, you read back. The brain does not work like that. Every time you remember something, you **rebuild** a scene out of fragments.
That is powerful, and it is fallible. Understanding it means understanding why we forget, why we get things wrong, and why we learn.

blocks.caption: Different areas of the brain handle different forms of memory

blocks.text: First comes [[working memory]]: what you hold in your head for a few seconds, like a phone number. It is limited, about **7 items** on average. Then comes **long-term memory**: facts, memories of events, and skills such as riding a bike.

These systems do not all live in the same part of the brain. The **prefrontal cortex**, the front part of the brain behind the forehead, does much of the work for working memory. Other regions, such as the **neocortex**, the outer layer of the brain, handle long-term storage.

blocks.caption: The hippocampus, a structure deep in the brain, helps form new memories

blocks.text: For a piece of information to go from fragile to lasting, the brain has to strengthen the connections between **neurons**, the nerve cells. This is called **consolidation**, the turning of a recent memory into a durable trace. A small structure called the **hippocampus**, shaped like a seahorse and tucked into the temporal lobe, plays a key role for memories of events.
Sleep, and some of its phases above all, helps lock in what you learned during the day. Studying and then sleeping usually beats studying until 3 a.m.

A famous rule, linked to the researcher **Donald Hebb**: neurons that fire together tend to connect more strongly. In short, “cells that fire together wire together.” That is the principle of **neuroplasticity**, the brain's ability to change its own connections.

When you call up a memory, it briefly becomes **malleable**, open to change. Details from the present can slip into it. Then the brain stores it again. That is why two witnesses to the same accident can tell different versions.
You can even create **false memories**: scenes you believe are true, but that never happened, or not that way. The brain fills the gaps with what it already knows.

sections.title: Forgetting is not always a failure

blocks.text: If you remembered every useless detail, you would be swamped. Forgetting helps you generalize, decide, and keep what matters. A good memory sorts as much as it stores.
Memory is an active reconstruction, not a perfect recording. It rests on several systems, it consolidates above all during sleep, and it can bend a little every time you call it up.
